title: Joseph Goebbels
subtitle: The propaganda minister who taught a nation to hate

package.intro: Joseph Goebbels never commanded an army or ran a camp. As Hitler's propaganda minister from 1933 to 1945, he controlled what Germans read, heard and watched, and used it to make hatred of Jews feel normal. This documentary tells how a rejected writer became the voice of the Nazi regime.
facts: Born 29 October 1897 in Rheydt, in the Rhineland
Rejected for military service in 1914 because of a deformed foot
Earned a doctorate from Heidelberg University in 1921
Became Nazi party chief (Gauleiter) of Berlin in November 1926
Appointed Reich Minister of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda in March 1933
His speech in Munich on 9 November 1938 set off the Kristallnacht pogrom
Gave the 'total war' speech at the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943
Named chancellor in Hitler's testament; on 1 May 1945 he and Magda Goebbels had their six children killed and then took their own lives
package.sources: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (Holocaust Encyclopedia), Encyclopaedia Britannica, Peter Longerich's Goebbels: A Biography, Toby Thacker's Joseph Goebbels: Life and Death, Richard J. Evans's Third Reich trilogy.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: JOSEPH GOEBBELS
lines.sub: The propaganda minister who taught a nation to hate

lines: On the evening of the eighteenth of February 1943, a small, thin man with a limp stepped up to the podium at the Berlin Sportpalast. In front of him sat thousands of hand-picked party loyalists.
He asked them a series of questions. The most famous was this: do you want total war? The crowd roared back that it did.
The speech went out on radio across Germany. It was theatre, staged by the man who had spent ten years deciding what Germans saw, read and heard.
Joseph Goebbels was Hitler's propaganda minister. He did not command armies or run the camps. His weapon was persuasion, and he used it to make hatred feel normal. This is how he did it.

sections.name: A rejected young man
lines: Paul Joseph Goebbels was born on the twenty-ninth of October 1897 in Rheydt, a textile town in western Germany. His family was Catholic, devout and of modest means.

lines.name: Joseph Goebbels
lines.role: Clever, ambitious and insecure. A doctor of literature and a failed writer.

lines: As a small boy he developed a deformed right foot, and he walked with a limp for the rest of his life. In 1914, when his classmates went off to war, the army turned him down.
He was a gifted student. He studied literature at several universities and earned a doctorate from Heidelberg in 1921. For the rest of his life, he liked to be called Doctor Goebbels.
He wanted to be a writer. He wrote a novel, plays and articles, and publishers turned almost all of them down. He drifted between short jobs, including one at a bank.

lines.head: Inflation
lines.sub: Savings wiped out across the country

lines: Germany was bitter and broke. In 1923, runaway inflation wiped out people's savings. Goebbels, resentful and searching for something to believe in, began to blame Jews for everything.

sections.name: Finding Hitler
lines: In 1924 he joined the Nazi movement. He worked for Gregor Strasser, a leader of the party's northern wing, which talked more about socialism than Hitler did.
At first, Goebbels was critical of Hitler. Then, in 1926, Hitler invited him to Munich, flattered him and won him over completely. His diary from that spring reads like a love letter.

lines.name: Gauleiter of Berlin
lines.role: Nazi party chief in the capital. Founded the newspaper The Attack.

lines: Hitler rewarded him. In November 1926, Goebbels became the party's chief in Berlin, a city where the Nazis were tiny and the left was strong.
He set out to get attention by any means. He provoked street brawls with communists and launched a newspaper called The Attack.
In 1930, a young stormtrooper named Horst Wessel was shot by communists. Goebbels turned him into a martyr, and a song Wessel had written became the party's anthem.

lines.place: Goebbels marries Magda Quandt · Hitler is a witness

lines: In December 1931 he married Magda Quandt, a wealthy divorcée. Hitler was a witness at the wedding. The couple would have six children.
That year Hitler made him head of party propaganda. In the elections of 1932, he flew Hitler from city to city to speak to vast crowds, a novelty at the time.

sections.name: The minister
lines: Weeks after Hitler became chancellor, Goebbels was given a new ministry: the Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. He was thirty-five years old.
In May 1933, students across Germany burned books by Jewish, left-wing and other banned writers. In Berlin, around twenty thousand books went into the flames, and Goebbels spoke beside the fire.
Within months he controlled the press, radio, film, theatre, music and art. Anyone who wanted to work in culture had to belong to a chamber under his ministry, and Jews were shut out.
He wanted a radio in every home. The regime promoted a cheap set called the People's Receiver, and millions were sold. Hitler's speeches could now reach almost everyone.
When Berlin hosted the Olympic Games in 1936, his ministry showed visitors a tidy, welcoming Germany. Some antisemitic signs were quietly taken down until the guests had gone.

lines.text: Name an enemy. Repeat it. Again.

lines: His method was simple. Keep the message short, emotional and endlessly repeated. Name an enemy. Celebrate the leader. Make doubt feel like betrayal.

sections.name: The enemy
lines: From the start, his chief target was Germany's Jews. In April 1933, he helped organise a nationwide boycott of Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers.
On the ninth of November 1938, after a young Jewish man shot a German diplomat in Paris, Goebbels gave a furious speech to party leaders in Munich. They took it as a signal to attack.

That night, mobs and stormtroopers burned synagogues and smashed Jewish shops and homes across Germany. At least ninety-one Jews were killed, and around thirty thousand men were sent to concentration camps.

lines.label: Reichsmarks · fine imposed on Germany's Jews after Kristallnacht

lines: Afterwards, the regime made Germany's Jews pay a collective fine of one billion Reichsmarks for the damage done to them.

sections.name: Total war
lines: When war came in 1939, his ministry became a war machine of its own. Newsreels in every cinema showed victory after victory.
Listening to foreign radio stations was made a crime. Some Germans were sentenced to death for passing on what they had heard.
His ministry made antisemitic films designed to make audiences fear and despise Jews. Millions of Germans watched them.
As Gauleiter of Berlin, he pushed for the city's Jews to be deported. In 1943 the regime declared the city free of Jews. Most of those deported were murdered.

lines.text: His diary shows he knew the deportations meant mass murder.
lines.who: summary of his diary entry, 27 March 1942

lines: He knew where they were going. In March 1942, he wrote in his diary that about sixty percent of the Jews being sent east would be liquidated. He called it barbaric, and deserved.
After the German defeat at Stalingrad in early 1943, he gave his total war speech. Luxury shops and restaurants were closed, and more people were pushed into factories and the army.

lines.name: Plenipotentiary for Total War
lines.role: Helped crush the July plot. Put in charge of mobilising the home front.

lines: In July 1944, when army officers tried to kill Hitler, Goebbels helped crush the coup in Berlin. Hitler rewarded him with control of total war mobilisation.

sections.name: The bunker
lines: By April 1945, Berlin was surrounded. Goebbels moved his family into Hitler's bunker, and he still told the city to fight on.
In his last testament, Hitler named Goebbels as chancellor. Hitler took his own life the next day. Goebbels held the title for about a day.
On the first of May, he and Magda had their six children, aged four to twelve, poisoned. That evening, the couple took their own lives.

lines.date: Helga · Hilde · Helmut · Holde · Hedda · Heide

lines: The children were Helga, Hilde, Helmut, Holde, Hedda and Heide. They had no say in any of it.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: Goebbels never faced a court. At Nuremberg, his radio chief, Hans Fritzsche, was acquitted. But Julius Streicher, publisher of a vicious antisemitic newspaper, was hanged for inciting persecution.
His diaries, kept for more than twenty years, survived the war. They are one of the most important sources historians have on how the Nazi regime worked.

lines.text: If you tell a lie big enough and keep repeating it, people will eventually come to believe it.
lines.who: often attributed to Goebbels · no source has ever been found

lines: A famous saying about the big lie is often credited to him. No historian has found it in his writings or speeches. Even his reputation has a little propaganda in it.
His real methods are well documented. Name an enemy, repeat it without end, silence anyone who disagrees, and make cruelty look ordinary.
Goebbels did not invent hatred of Jews. What he showed is how quickly a state that controls every screen and speaker can teach millions of people to accept it.
